title: Pow(x, n)
directAnswer: Compute xⁿ in O(log n) using fast (binary) exponentiation: square the base and halve the exponent each step, multiplying the result in only when the current exponent bit is 1. Handle negative n by computing the positive power and returning its reciprocal — but convert n to a long FIRST, because negating INT_MIN (-2³¹) overflows a 32-bit int.

remember.pattern: Fast exponentiation — square the base, halve the exponent
remember.formula:
xⁿ = (x²)^(n/2)        if n even
xⁿ = x · (x²)^(n/2)   if n odd
x⁻ⁿ = 1 / xⁿ
# in code: long N = n; if N<0: x = 1/x, N = -N
rules: **Promote n to a `long` before negating** — `-INT_MIN` overflows a 32-bit int. This is THE bug interviewers wait for.
**For negative n, take the reciprocal**: `x⁻ⁿ = 1 / xⁿ`. Either flip `x = 1/x` once at the start, or compute `xⁿ` and return `1 / result`.
**Square the base, halve the exponent** every iteration — that's what turns O(n) multiplications into O(log n).
**Multiply the running result in only when the exponent is odd** (lowest bit set). Even exponents just keep squaring.
**n = 0 returns 1** for any x (including x = 0 by convention here). Make sure the loop/recursion bottoms out at 1.
**Iterative avoids stack overflow**; recursive is cleaner to explain. Both are O(log n) — know both.
whenToUse: Raising to an integer power and naive O(n) multiplication is too slow
Exponent can be huge (10⁹+) — you need O(log n)
Modular exponentiation (a^b mod m) — same skeleton, mod each multiply
Any 'apply an associative operation n times' (matrix power, fast Fibonacci)
antiSignals: Exponent is tiny / bounded by a small constant → a simple loop is fine and clearer
Base or exponent is floating/non-integer → use the library `pow` / logarithms
You only need x² or x³ → just multiply directly, no need for the trick
Language has a trusted bignum pow and the interview allows it
remember.takeaway: Binary exponentiation is the canonical 'do something n times in log n steps' tool: exploit that the operation is associative and that n's binary representation tells you exactly which squared powers to multiply. The same skeleton powers modular exponentiation, matrix exponentiation, and fast Fibonacci.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know the O(log n) doubling trick instead of looping n times, can reason about associativity, and — critically — whether you spot the INT_MIN negation overflow when handling negative exponents.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Negating n with `n = -n` while n is still a 32-bit int, overflowing on n = -2³¹; or looping n times for an O(n) solution that times out on large exponents.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the recurrence (x^n = (x^2)^(n/2)), explain why it's O(log n), promote n to long before negating, and mention the same pattern generalizes to modular and matrix exponentiation.

problemStatement:
Implement `pow(x, n)`, which calculates `x` raised to the power `n` (i.e., `xⁿ`).

`x` is a floating-point number and `n` is a signed 32-bit integer that may be **negative**.
constraints: n is an integer; either x is not zero or n > 0
understanding: Raise a floating-point base x to an integer power n that can be negative or as large as ~2.1 billion. A loop of n multiplications is far too slow for big n, so we need the O(log n) doubling method. Negative n means a reciprocal, and n = -2³¹ has no positive counterpart in 32 bits — that edge case must be handled with a wider type.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can n be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. xⁿ for negative n is 1 / x^|n|. So compute the positive power and take the reciprocal.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 2³¹ − 1 ≈ 2.1 billion, and down to -2³¹. A naive O(n) loop would time out, and negating -2³¹ overflows a 32-bit int — handle with a long.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What is x⁰?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 1 for any x by convention (the problem guarantees we never hit 0⁰ in a problematic way). The recursion/loop must bottom out returning 1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Floating-point precision — exact or approximate?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Approximate is accepted; results within 10⁻⁵ are fine. We don't need exact decimal arithmetic.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree. Pow(x, n) needs the O(log n) doubling branch — looping n times times out.

approaches.name: Recursive Divide & Conquer
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this — it makes the O(log n) recurrence visually obvious and is the easiest to explain on a whiteboard.
hints: Naively xⁿ = x · x · … (n times) is O(n). Can you compute xⁿ from a SMALLER power so the work shrinks fast?
Note xⁿ = (x^(n/2))². If you compute the half-power once and square it, you halve the exponent each call — that's a log-depth recursion.
Handle odd n by peeling one factor: xⁿ = x · (x^(n/2))² when n is odd. And for negative n, compute x^|n| and return its reciprocal — but convert n to long before negating to dodge INT_MIN overflow.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each recursive call halves n, so the recursion depth is log₂|n|. One multiplication per level → O(log n) time. The call stack is log n deep → O(log n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The key algebraic identity is `xⁿ = (x^(n/2))²`. Computing the half-power **once** and squaring it does the work of the full power in a single extra multiply — and since the exponent halves every call, we reach the base case in `log₂ n` steps instead of `n`.

**Why squaring the half is the whole speedup.** Naive exponentiation multiplies `x` into an accumulator `n` times — linear work. Divide-and-conquer instead asks: "what if I already knew `x^(n/2)`?" Then `xⁿ` is just that value squared. The recursion computes `half = pow(x, n/2)` once and reuses it twice via `half * half`, so each level of recursion does constant multiplications and there are only `log n` levels. That reuse — compute once, square — is the entire reason the exponent collapses logarithmically.

**Handling odd exponents.** Integer division loses the remainder: for odd `n`, `n/2` rounds down, so `(x^(n/2))²` gives `x^(n-1)`. We're short exactly one factor of `x`, so we multiply it back: `n` odd → `x · half · half`. For even `n` no correction is needed. This is the recursive mirror of "multiply in only when the bit is 1".

**The negative-exponent trap — and why `long` matters.** For `n < 0`, `xⁿ = 1 / x^|n|`. The obvious move is `n = -n`, then compute the positive power and reciprocate. But `n` can be `-2³¹ = -2147483648`, and `+2147483648` does **not** fit in a signed 32-bit int — negating it overflows and wraps right back to `-2147483648`, causing an infinite recursion or wrong sign. The fix is to widen `n` to a 64-bit `long` *before* negating, so `2147483648L` is representable. In Python integers are unbounded so this is a non-issue, but you must still call it out for the Java/C++ interviewer.
approaches.insight: `xⁿ = (x^(n/2))²` is the divide-and-conquer heart: compute the subproblem once, square it, and the exponent halves every level. The odd-n correction (`× x`) and the negative-n reciprocal are the two bookkeeping details — and the `long` promotion before negating is the trap that separates a passing solution from a robust one.

dryRun.intro: Each call halves n. Compute the half-power once, then square it; multiply an extra x only when n is odd.

steps.action: n even → half = pow(2,5), return half²
n even → half = pow(2,1), return half²

java.explanation: Promote to long BEFORE negating — -INT_MIN overflows a 32-bit int.
Negative exponent → reciprocal base, then treat the exponent as positive.
Compute the half-power ONCE and reuse it — this is the O(log n) speedup.
Odd exponent lost a factor in integer division — multiply x back in.

python.explanation: Base case: anything to the 0 is 1, terminating the recursion.
Single recursive call on half the exponent — squared below for reuse.
Odd exponent → square the half and multiply one extra base.
Python ints are unbounded so no overflow, but still flip to reciprocal for negative n.

diagrams.title: Recursion tree halving the exponent
diagrams.caption: Each call halves n; depth is log₂ n. The half-power is computed once and squared.

edgeCases.behavior: long N = n makes N = -2147483648; N = -N becomes 2147483648 (fits in long). Without the long, this overflows back to negative.
1 to any power is 1; recursion bottoms out quickly with all multiplications equal to 1.

pitfalls: Negating n while it's still an int — overflow on n = -2³¹.
Recomputing pow(x, n/2) twice instead of storing it once — degrades to O(n).
Forgetting the odd-n extra ×x — gives x^(n-1) for odd exponents.

approaches.name: Iterative Binary Exponentiation (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the production-grade version: same O(log n) time but O(1) space and no stack-overflow risk on huge exponents.
hints: Write n in binary. xⁿ is the product of x^(2^k) for every bit k that is set in n. Can you accumulate that product while scanning the bits?
Keep a running `result = 1` and a `current = x`. Each step: if the lowest bit of n is 1, multiply `result *= current`; then square `current *= current` and shift n right (n /= 2).
Convert n to long and handle negativity up front (x = 1/x, n = -n). Loop while n > 0. This is the same math as the recursion but with no call stack.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n has ~log₂ n bits; we do O(1) work per bit (a compare, maybe a multiply, a square, a shift). So O(log n) time and only a few scalar variables → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
This is the same doubling math as the recursion, expressed by walking the **binary representation of n**. Every integer `n` is a sum of distinct powers of two — its set bits — so `xⁿ` is the product of `x` raised to each of those powers: `x^(2^0)`, `x^(2^1)`, `x^(2^2)`, … We generate those squared powers on the fly and multiply in only the ones whose bit is set.

**The two state variables.** `current` starts at `x` and is **squared every iteration**, so it walks through `x¹, x², x⁴, x⁸, …` — exactly the `x^(2^k)` values. `result` starts at `1` and accumulates the answer. At each step we look at the lowest bit of `n`: if it's `1`, the current squared power belongs in the product, so `result *= current`. Then we square `current` and shift `n` right by one bit (`n /= 2`) to examine the next bit. When `n` hits `0`, every set bit has contributed and `result` holds `xⁿ`.

**Why this equals the recursion.** The recursive `(x^(n/2))²` and this `square-current-each-step` are two views of the same identity. Halving the exponent in the recursion corresponds to shifting `n` right by a bit here; squaring the half corresponds to squaring `current`. The iterative form just makes the exponent's binary structure explicit and drops the call stack — turning O(log n) **space** into O(1) space, which also removes any stack-overflow risk for exponents in the billions.

**Negative exponent, same trap.** As before, `n < 0` means reciprocate: set `x = 1/x` and make `n` positive. And again, promote `n` to a `long` before negating so `-2³¹` doesn't overflow. After that the loop is identical. This iterative skeleton is also the one you extend for **modular exponentiation** — just take `% m` after each multiply — and for **matrix exponentiation** by replacing scalar multiply with matrix multiply.
approaches.insight: Reading n in binary makes the algorithm obvious: each set bit picks one squared power x^(2^k) to include. `result` collects the chosen powers, `current` marches through the powers of two by self-squaring. This O(1)-space loop is the template you reuse verbatim for modular and matrix exponentiation.

dryRun.intro: 10 in binary is 1010. result starts at 1, current at 2. Multiply result by current only when the low bit is 1, then square current and shift n.

steps.action: low bit 0 → no multiply; square current 2→4; n→5
low bit 1 → result=1·4=4; square current 4→16; n→2
low bit 0 → no multiply; square current 16→256; n→1
low bit 1 → result=4·256=1024; square current; n→0

java.explanation: Widen before negating — -INT_MIN doesn't fit in a 32-bit int.
Lowest bit set means this power of two is part of n — include current in the product.
Square to move from x^(2^k) to x^(2^(k+1)) for the next bit.
Shift right to examine the next exponent bit.

python.explanation: Negative exponent → reciprocal base and positive exponent (no overflow in Python).
Odd → current squared-power contributes to the result.
Self-square walks current through x¹, x², x⁴, x⁸, …
Drop the bit we just processed and move on.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop body never runs (0 > 0 false); result stays 1.0 — correct for x⁰.
current = 0, result becomes 0 on the first set bit; returns 0.0.
long N negates safely to 2147483648; loop runs ~31 times. An int negation here would overflow.

pitfalls: Negating n as an int — overflow on -2³¹ before the loop even starts.
Squaring current AFTER shifting n, or in the wrong order relative to the multiply — keep multiply, then square, then shift.
Using `result *= x` instead of `result *= current` — loses the doubling and gives wrong powers.

commonMistakes: Looping n times — O(n) and times out for n in the billions.
Negating n while it's a 32-bit int — overflows on n = -2³¹.
Recomputing the half-power twice in the recursion, degrading to O(n).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: INT_MIN negation overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: n can be -2³¹. Negating it as a 32-bit int wraps back to -2³¹, causing infinite recursion or a wrong result. Promote to long first.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: O(n) loop times out
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Multiplying x into an accumulator n times is linear; with n up to ~2.1 billion it TLEs. Use the log-n doubling instead.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recomputing the half-power
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Calling pow(x, n/2) twice (once per occurrence of the square) doubles the recursion at every level, collapsing O(log n) back to O(n).
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
double half = fastPow(x, n / 2);
return half * half;

followupVariations.hint: The inverse — find the integer whose square is ≤ x via binary search.

followupVariations.title: Count Good Numbers
followupVariations.hint: Direct application of modular fast exponentiation under a prime modulus.

followupVariations.title: Fibonacci Number
followupVariations.hint: Matrix exponentiation gives O(log n) Fibonacci using the same doubling skeleton.

patternNote: Binary (fast) exponentiation — the canonical divide-and-conquer for repeated associative operations. Recognise it whenever you must apply something n times and n is large: scalar power, modular power (a^b mod m), matrix power (fast Fibonacci). Square the operand, halve the exponent, multiply in on set bits.
